name: Apache
packetScope: Four renewed substantive historical/community works: Plains Apache/Oklahoma, Fort Sill Chiricahua, Mescalero and the publishing Lipan Apache Tribe. These are separate situated perspectives within the broad Apache entry, not one government. No canonical/Site edits, contact or delegation.

sources.annotation: Everett's dated reference supports the Plains Apache discussion while acknowledging contradictory scholarship. claimBlocks.suggestedSection: Plains Apache identity and historical scholarship
claimBlocks.text: Dianna Everett's 2010 history describes the Apache Tribe of Oklahoma as a distinct linguistic and cultural community despite long relationships with other Plains peoples. Her account connects bison hunting with later reservation confinement and allotment, while acknowledging disagreements among historical and ethnographic interpretations. This Plains Apache history is a specific regional trajectory. It should be read alongside community perspectives, with the tribe kept distinct from Fort Sill's Chiricahua descendants.
claimBlocks.sourceLocator: Article paragraphs on Plains livelihoods and scholarship, lines 99–104

claimBlocks.suggestedSection: Fort Sill Chiricahua displacement and settlement
claimBlocks.text: Fort Sill Apache history describes Chiricahua people arriving in Oklahoma in 1894 after imprisonment in Florida and Alabama. Its account follows pressure to leave the military reservation and different responses: some relocated to Mescalero in 1913, while others continued seeking promised lands near Fort Sill. It dates the latter group's release and resettlement on Oklahoma allotments to 1914. These forced movements explain distinct community histories rather than a single relocation shared by all Apache peoples.

The Mescalero Apache Tribe identifies Mescalero, Lipan and Chiricahua within its community. Its historical account dates the reservation's establishment to May 29, 1873, and describes Lipan arrivals from northern Chihuahua around 1903 and Chiricahua arrivals in 1913. These accounts connect the reservation with distinct histories of displacement and community formation. Membership in this government should not be equated with every Lipan or Chiricahua person's political belonging, or its cultural account applied to all Apache peoples.

claimBlocks.suggestedSection: A Lipan government's account of Texas and Mexico
claimBlocks.text: The Lipan Apache Tribe's public history follows movement between Texas and Mexico under pressure and describes surviving communities around San Antonio, the Rio Grande Valley and Big Bend. Its narrative emphasizes continuity through displacement rather than disappearance. The page's description of a united community concerns this publishing tribe's own organization. It provides one Lipan governmental perspective, which should remain distinct from Mescalero membership and other Lipan voices.
claimBlocks.sourceLocator: Our Sacred History, cross-border and community-continuity paragraphs 31–34

inspectionNotes.method: Actual authored article, byline, displayed January 15, 2010 date and footer read directly.
inspectionNotes.materialIssue: Introductory line 98 loosely conflates Chiricahua/Western Apache and locates Fort Sill imprisonment in Indian Territory in the 1880s. Fort Sill's actual own history states transfer to Oklahoma in 1894. Do not use the erroneous aside for naming or chronology.
inspectionNotes.limits: Article's described language projects and 2000 enrollment are not current findings. Cited books/dissertations and underlying fieldwork remain unread. No source file downloaded. Footer copyright/linking assertion recorded transparently without presenting it as a licence.

Reservation proclamation and 2013–2014 litigation appear in its institutional account, but no statutory text, executive order or court judgment was independently read here. No current law, entitlement, casino authority or population inference.

inspectionNotes.method: Actual selected historical sections read beyond introductory branding. Later body was screened only to exclude sensitive/unneeded detail.
inspectionNotes.materialIssue: The page's later biographies and compressed prisoner narrative contain potential chronology problems. Do not repeat its statement implying Chiricahua were at Fort Sill continuously from 1886; the Fort Sill history gives 1894 arrival. Selected synthesis relies only on composition and arrival paragraphs.
inspectionNotes.limits: No sacred narrative, ceremonial sequence, animal-related prescription, plant preparation, burial location, casualty total or present council/term claim. The 1873 executive order itself was not read in this packet.

inspectionNotes.method: Actual full history and institutional self-identification read. No search-only evidence or directory substituted.
inspectionNotes.limits: Origins/timelines remain the publisher's account; no precise ancient migration chronology adopted. The website's sovereign/state-recognition and feather-case descriptions were not independently legally verified. No inference that every Lipan descendant belongs to one tribe or that 2019 resolutions confer a particular present federal status.

integrationNotes: All four are renewals. Map ae16-h1→p16-s1, ae16-h2→p16-s4, ae16-h3→p16-s5, ae16-h4→p16-s6; preserve original URLs and do not count old/new cards separately.

Use replacement blocks rather than appending to old mixed-source paragraphs. Existing p16-s1,p16-s4,p16-s5 each support several long sections; retain no duplicate legacy body without recomputing the full 180-word/work budget, including overview and subresource scopes.

The old Mescalero-linked language/cultural paragraph should not survive automatically through this historical renewal. This packet does not propose ceremonial description; keep language-program evidence with its separately reviewed community-specific source.

Plains/Kiowa Apache, Fort Sill Chiricahua, Mescalero's government, Lipan Apache Tribe's self-account and other Lipan communities remain distinct. No separate people or governmental membership is inferred from a broad language label alone.

OHS is a substantive reference with a material excluded aside and an observed restrictive copyright/linking statement. Root may retain it as a scoped reference or reduce it to supporting context; do not silently turn this review into an assurance of media/text reuse rights.
Do not add a current recognition, citizenship, resource-use or individual eligibility rule from these historical pages. No new source quota, source media, contact or full-profile completion claim.
researchGaps: Primary legal instruments and original confinement/allotment records were not read in this bounded renewal; institutional legal summaries are not a substitute.
Additional Plains Apache-authored public histories and other Lipan community voices would broaden the present institutional selection.
Current programs, political memberships, speaker totals and outcomes require dated evidence. These historical pages do not establish them.
Ceremonial knowledge, sensitive locations, family records and source media remain outside the proposed synthesis.
